newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-S&P puts Thailand on negative credit watch.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-S&P puts Thailand on negative credit watch.

text.p: Standard & Poor's Corp said on Friday it has placed Thailand's "A" long-term foreign currency rating on creditwatch with negative implications.

S&P said about US$3 billion of foreign currency debt was affected. The international ratings agency said it had also placed Thailand's "AA" long-term local currency credit rating on creditwatch with negative implications.

The creditwatch placement reflected greater than expected loan losses in the financial sector, which were expected to put a sizeable fiscal burden on the government and lead to weakened economic growth for several years, it said.
"So far, Thailand's weak coalition government has been slow to recognise and effectively manage problems in the financial sector," S&P said.
"An erosion of investor confidence, in turn, has intensified balance of payments pressures and tight domestic liquidity conditions, despite the recent depreciation of the Thai baht."
The credit rating agency said the creditwatch status would be resolved over the next month following a review of:
- the potential scale of problem loans of commercial banks, and of finance and securities companies;
- the intensity of financial stress on the corporate sector, and prospects for an export led economic recovery;
- the government's financial sector restructuring package expected to be announced next week; and
- the proposed economic stabilisation and reform programme with the International Monetary Fund.
"The review will focus primarily on the likely cost to the government of financial sector support operations," S&P said.

"The restoration of financial system soundness hinges on the recognition of the true level of bad loans, a comprehensive programme to strengthen the capitalisation of the financial system, and decisive implementation of measures adopted.

"Signs of a rapid economic recovery could ease ongoing stress on the financial sector, lower the cost of bail-out operations, and stablise Thailand's credit standing at current rating levels," S&P said.
"Under a worse-case scenario, the long-term local currency and foreign currency ratings of the Kingdom would fall no lower than to AA-minus and A-minus respectively," it said.
S&P said high corporate and household indebtedness, at about 150 percent of gross domestic product this year, underscored the private sector's vulnerability to the current economic slowdown.

"While Thailand's credit standing continues to be supported by low public sector indebtedness, the fiscal and economic costs of problem loans will weaken the government's financial flexibility and test macro-economics management in the medium term," it said.
"Equally important, deteriorating asset quality is likely to keep credit scarce and expensive, and could prolong the economic slowdown to beyond 1998," S&P said.
